stem: If $n$ is the number of antibody kits in the order, what is the greatest possible value of $n$?
stimulus: An immunology lab is placing one order of assay kits and can spend at most $\$2{,}000$. The order must include at least $12$ cytokine kits, which cost $\$65$ each. All other kits in the order are antibody kits, which cost $\$48$ each. A flat $\$90$ shipping fee is charged on the whole order. The lab's freezer can store no more than $32$ kits in total.
explanation: To get the most antibody kits, you buy only the required $12$ cytokine kits, because each extra cytokine kit costs money and takes up freezer space. Budget: $90 + 12(65) + 48n \le 2{,}000$, so $48n \le 1{,}130$ and $n \le 23.54$, which gives $n \le 23$. Freezer: $12 + n \le 32$, so $n \le 20$. Both conditions have to hold, so the freezer limit is the one that decides it, and the greatest possible value is $n = 20$. That order costs $90 + 780 + 960 = \$1{,}830$, which is within the budget.

B.why: You solved the budget inequality correctly and rounded down, but you stopped there. With $12$ cytokine kits and $23$ antibody kits, the order has $35$ kits, which is more than the freezer's limit of $32$.

C.why: You rounded $23.54$ up to $24$. For a maximum you have to round down, because $24$ antibody kits would cost $90 + 780 + 1{,}152 = \$2{,}022$, which is over budget. You also didn't check the freezer limit.

D.why: You left out the $\$90$ shipping fee and solved $780 + 48n \le 2{,}000$, which gives $n \le 25.4$. The fee is part of the total, and this answer also breaks the freezer limit.

stem: What is the least possible value of $p$?
stimulus: A printmaker is making an edition of $p$ linocut prints. Carving the block costs $\$140$, and paper and ink cost $\$5$ per print. Each print sells for $\$20$, but the gallery keeps $25\%$ of the price of every print it sells. Assume every print sells. The printmaker wants the edition's profit to be more than $\$400$.
explanation: The printmaker keeps $75\%$ of $\$20$, which is $\$15$ per print. After paying $\$5$ for materials, each print earns $\$10$. Profit is $10p - 140$, so you need $10p - 140 > 400$. That gives $10p > 540$, so $p > 54$. Because the inequality is strict, $54$ prints is not enough: the profit would be exactly $\$400$. The least whole-number value is $p = 55$.

A.why: You subtracted $140$ from $400$ instead of adding it, so you got $10p > 260$ and $p > 26$. To isolate $10p$, you have to add the block cost to both sides.

B.why: You left out the gallery's $25\%$ cut and used $\$15$ per print ($20 - 5$), which gives $15p > 540$ and $p > 36$. The printmaker only receives $\$15$ of each sale, so materials leave $\$10$, not $\$15$.

C.why: You solved $p > 54$ correctly and then kept the boundary value. At $p = 54$ the profit is exactly $\$400$, which does not satisfy *more than* $\$400$. The strict inequality means you have to go up to the next whole number.
